notes.meaning: Jesse was the father of King David. Although David's royal line seemed cut down like a dead tree stump, a fresh green shoot would sprout from its roots. This promised ruler is the Messiah, Jesus Christ, who came from humble beginnings to bring new life.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars suggest that naming Jesse instead of David points to a brand-new start for the royal line, like a new David, rather than just another failing king in David's family line.

notes.meaning: God's Holy Spirit will rest permanently on this King. The Spirit equips Him with deep wisdom, the skill to make good plans, the power to carry them out, and a reverent love for God.

differ.view: John Calvin argued that this passage lists six gifts of the Spirit rather than seven, and that Christ received these gifts to share them with His people.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic tradition counts seven gifts of the Holy Spirit here by including piety (godliness), following the ancient Greek and Latin translations of this verse.

notes.meaning: The Messiah will find His joy in honoring and obeying the Lord. He will not judge people by outward looks or make decisions based on rumors, because He sees straight into the human heart.
This King will defend the poor and protect humble people who cannot defend themselves. With the authority of His word, He will bring justice to the earth and put an end to the wicked.
Righteousness and faithfulness wrap around Him like a strong belt. Just as a royal sash holds clothing in place for action, doing what is right and true defines everything He does.

Fierce animals and gentle farm animals will live together in complete safety. Even dangerous snakes will not harm little children playing near their dens. This picture shows the wonderful peace and security that the Messiah brings to the world.

differ.view: Premillennial interpreters expect a literal renewal of the animal kingdom and physical nature when Christ returns to reign on earth.
Many Reformed interpreters see this as a picture of the gospel changing fierce human hearts, or as a promise of the final new creation rather than an earthly thousand-year reign.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view this animal peace as poetic imagery describing human society freed from every kind of oppressor.

notes.meaning: On God's holy mountain, which represents His church and kingdom, there will be no harm or evil. Just as waters fill every part of the ocean bed, knowledge of the Lord and love for Him will cover the entire earth.
The Messiah, coming from the family line of Jesse, will stand like a raised banner for all peoples to see. Nations from all over the world will seek Him out, and His resting place will be glorious.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Following the Latin Vulgate translation, Catholic tradition often understood the Messiah's glorious rest as a reference to His holy tomb.

notes.meaning: God promises to reach out His hand to rescue the surviving remnant of His scattered people from distant lands. Just as He brought Israel out of Egypt long ago, He will perform an even greater rescue for His people.

differ.view: Premillennial interpreters believe this promises a future, worldwide physical gathering of ethnic Jewish people back to their land under Christ.
Reformed commentators traditionally see this fulfilled as Christ calls Jewish and Gentile believers from across the earth into His church.

notes.meaning: The Lord will lift up a signal banner for the nations and bring His scattered people home. Both men and women from Israel and Judah will be gathered from the four corners of the earth into His kingdom.
The old, bitter jealousy between the northern kingdom of Ephraim and the southern kingdom of Judah will end. God's people will no longer fight one another, but will live together in love and unity.

The reunited people of God will overcome the old enemies that once surrounded them, from the Philistines in the west to Edom, Moab, and Ammon in the east. Ancient foes will no longer be able to oppress God's people.

differ.view: John Wesley and other Methodist commentators explain this as a spiritual victory won when Christ's ministers spread the gospel among all nations.

notes.meaning: God will remove every great barrier that stands in the way of His people coming home, just as He parted the Red Sea. He will sweep away dangerous waters and divide rivers into shallow streams so travelers can cross dry-shod.

A clear highway will be opened for the surviving remnant of God's people returning from Assyria. Their homecoming will be like the miraculous road God made through the sea when Israel escaped from Egypt.
